variables.PATH_WIDTH: Medium uniform weight (around three to four points, roughly six pixels at a thousand-pixel longest edge)

color_law_read_this_first: This worksheet has ONE absolute color law that overrides everything else in this prompt: in every stage, the parts of the character that were drawn in any earlier stage appear in light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}}, and only the parts freshly added in that stage appear in pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}.

The first stage is the only stage with all-black content, because nothing is older than it. Every other stage must contain gray. Every other stage must contain black. Every other stage must contain both.
The final stage is the stage with the MOST gray content and the LEAST black content — it is not a clean finished drawing in pure black.

Only two ink colors may appear on the character itself: pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}} and light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}}. Arrows between stages use {{ARROW_COLOR}}. No other grays, no other colors, no fills, no shading, no gradients.
prompt.task: Create a clean, premium-quality, print-ready step-by-step drawing worksheet that teaches a child in {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}} how to draw a {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} in exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} progressive stages, following the color law above. The final image must look like a polished page from a children's how-to-draw activity book that a real child can follow with a pencil — every stage must be physically drawable on top of the previous one without ever erasing.
hard_constraints: Render exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} progressive drawing stages — never fewer, never more.

Scale lock: every stage depicts the same character at the same size. The silhouette bounding box is identical in every stage. A stage with fewer lines must never appear smaller than a stage with more lines.

Identity lock: every stage depicts the same species, same breed, same pose, same expression, same accessories, same silhouette. No species drift. No accessory or distinguishing mark appearing mid-sequence.

Stroke rules: every line — whether pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}} or light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} — is exactly {{PATH_WIDTH}}, uniform from start to end. Gray lines are NOT thinner, softer, or fainter than black lines. Only the color value differs. No tapering, no pressure variation, no thinner detail lines, no thicker outer outlines.

Strict accumulation with recoloring: each stage is treated as a pixel-identical copy of the previous stage with two changes only — (a) every line that was pure black in the previous stage is recolored to light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} in this stage, and (b) freshly added lines in this stage are pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}. Never redraw, resize, rotate, translate, mirror, smooth, simplify, sharpen, clean up, refine, restyle, replace, or reinterpret any line that already appeared in an earlier stage. If you need a previously drawn line in a later stage, you reuse the exact same line — same coordinates, same length, same curvature, same endpoints, same thickness — only its color flips from black to gray.

Orientation lock: the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} faces the same direction in every single stage of the worksheet. The character is never flipped horizontally (left-right mirrored) and never flipped vertically (upside-down mirrored) between stages. If the character faces left in stage one, it faces left in every following stage. If it faces right in stage one, it faces right in every following stage. Same head tilt, same body angle, same eye direction, same nose direction, same tail direction, same paw or limb orientation in every stage.

Color-history lock: a line is pure black in exactly ONE stage (the stage in which it was introduced) and light gray in every stage after. A gray line never goes back to black in any later stage. Within a single stage, every individual line is ENTIRELY pure black or ENTIRELY light gray — never partially both, never blended, never gradient.

No-erase rule: a child following these stages with a pencil must never have to erase or modify any line they already drew. Every later stage must add new lines that fit cleanly around or attach to existing lines without crossing through, replacing, or contradicting them.
Background is fully {{BACKGROUND}} across the entire canvas, pure and uniform, with no transparency, no off-white, no cream, and no paper texture.
No text, letters, digits, captions, labels, titles, logos, or watermarks anywhere on the canvas. No stage numbers.
stage_to_stage_visual_continuity_critica: READ THIS BEFORE DRAWING ANY STAGE. The single most important rule of this worksheet is visual continuity from one stage to the next. A child must be able to look at any stage and see THE EXACT SAME DRAWING they saw in the previous stage — every line in exactly the same place — with the only differences being that the previously-black lines have faded to gray and a few fresh black lines have been added on top.

Mental model: imagine that stage one was drawn on a real sheet of paper in pure black ink. To produce stage two, that exact sheet of paper is photocopied 1:1 onto a fresh sheet, but the photocopier reproduces the previous black lines in light gray instead of black. Then, and only then, are the new stage-two lines drawn on top of the photocopy in fresh pure black. To produce stage three, the stage-two sheet is photocopied 1:1 again with the same gray-fade effect (so the previous-stage black lines now also fade to gray, joining the already-gray older lines), and the new stage-three lines are added on top in fresh black. And so on. Every stage is the gray-faded photocopy of the previous stage plus only the new black strokes of that stage. There is no other source of difference between stages.

Every line introduced in any earlier stage must remain in every following stage with all of these properties IDENTICAL: position on the canvas, length, width, height, orientation, rotation, curvature, smoothness, every bump and every dip, every endpoint, every junction with another line, and line thickness. The only thing that changes about an earlier line is its color: it becomes light gray from the stage immediately after the one in which it was introduced, and it stays light gray forever after. Not approximately the same shape — exactly the same shape.

Do not improve, polish, neaten, smooth, round, sharpen, simplify, regularize, symmetrize, beautify, redraw more carefully, or visually upgrade any earlier line in a later stage. Even if the earlier line looks slightly imperfect or could be drawn better, it must be reproduced unchanged in shape and only recolored to gray. The earlier stage is the source of truth — never the target of revision.

Do not nudge, shift, slide, drift, recenter, rebalance, re-anchor, or reposition any earlier line by even a single pixel. The character's anchor point in stage two is exactly the anchor point of stage one. The character's anchor point in stage three is exactly the anchor point of stage two. And so on.

Do not rescale any earlier line. The head circle from stage one is the same circle in stage two — same diameter, same center, same shape, same outline thickness — only recolored from black to gray. Not slightly larger, not slightly smaller, not slightly rounder, not slightly more oval.

Do not flip, mirror, or change the facing direction of the character or any of its parts between stages. The whole character keeps the exact same orientation in every stage — never horizontally mirrored (left to right or right to left), never vertically mirrored (upside down or right side up swap), never rotated by any angle. Every individual line keeps the exact same direction it had when first drawn: a curve that opens to the left in stage one still opens to the left in every later stage; a tail that sweeps to the right in an early stage still sweeps to the right in every later stage; a face looking left in an early stage still looks left in every later stage. Mirroring the character as a whole, or mirroring any part of it, is treated as a complete failure of the worksheet.

Do not restyle any earlier line. If stage one's head outline has a particular wobble or a particular curve, stage two's head outline has that exact same wobble and that exact same curve, only recolored to gray. Do not switch from a hand-drawn feel to a vector feel between stages, or from a slightly loose curve to a perfect arc, or from one line weight to another.

Do not re-ink, retrace, double-line, or re-outline any previously-drawn line in a later stage. A line that was already drawn in an earlier stage must not be drawn again over the top of itself in black or in any color. The next stage's black ink only goes onto FRESH areas of the page that no previous line has touched.

When a later stage adds a feature that touches or attaches to an earlier (now gray) line, the new black feature must connect to the earlier gray line at the exact endpoints already present in that line, with the earlier gray line itself remaining 100% unchanged in shape. Do not extend, shorten, or re-end any earlier line to make the connection cleaner — instead, plan the earlier line so the connection is already clean.

If at any point you find yourself wanting to redraw an earlier line because the new feature would fit better, STOP. The correct fix is never to redraw the earlier line — the correct fix is to go back and re-plan the earlier stage so the line was placed correctly from the start.

Stage validation test: if you mentally subtract a later stage from the previous stage, the only differences must be (a) every previously-black line is now gray, and (b) freshly added lines of the later stage are black. Subtracting must NEVER reveal that an earlier line moved, resized, rotated, smoothed, mirrored, or changed style. If subtraction reveals any change to an earlier line beyond the black-to-gray recolor, the worksheet is wrong and must be redone.

Forbidden continuity failures: head circle slightly larger or smaller in a later stage; body oval slightly more rounded or more elongated in a later stage; an earlier wobbly outline replaced with a smoother one in a later stage; a feature in a later stage drawn over the earlier line as a corrected version; the character drifting a few pixels left, right, up, or down between stages; the character's center of gravity shifting between stages; the line weight of an earlier line getting thicker or thinner in a later stage; an earlier line being broken into segments or fused into one continuous curve in a later stage; an earlier line still appearing in pure black in a later stage instead of gray; a previously-gray line turning back to black in a still-later stage.
step_to_step_completion_ease: When planning each stage, think about how the NEXT stage will be added by a child holding a pencil. The child should look at the current stage, immediately see where the new black lines belong, and be able to add them naturally — without confusion, without erasing, and without having to interpret an unusual or broken-looking base shape.

What actually makes a stage easy to continue is good PROPORTION and good POSITION of the base shapes — not literal pre-cut gaps in the outline. A head drawn at the right size and position already implies where ears, mane, hair, eyes, or a muzzle will go. A body drawn at the right length and angle already implies where legs and tail will go. The child reads these implied attachment zones automatically.

Default to clean, simple, friendly closed silhouettes in every early stage. A clean closed oval head is correct, even when ears, mane, or hair will be added later — children naturally draw ears that sit on top of a head and hair that flows along a head curve. They do NOT need a pre-cut notch to know where to put a new feature.

Do NOT damage the base silhouette with awkward notches, sudden cuts, slits, scoops, or unexplained gaps just because a future feature will attach there. A broken-looking base shape confuses the child far more than a clean closed shape ever does. A child seeing a strange slit in stage one will not understand why it is there and will not know what to do with it.

Two completion patterns are equally valid; choose whichever produces the cleanest, most child-friendly worksheet for the subject: (1) the new black feature in the later stage attaches OUTSIDE the earlier (now gray) closed shape, touching its outline cleanly along the surface (ears sitting on top of a closed head, legs dropping from a closed body, a tail curling away from a closed body, hair lying along the top of a closed head, a mane flowing down the side of a closed neck); (2) the new black feature in the later stage sits ENTIRELY INSIDE the earlier (now gray) closed shape (eyes, nose, mouth, cheeks, spots, simple inner markings, fur swirls). Both are good. Closed clean silhouettes are the safe default.

Only use a genuinely open shape (for example a cup drawn as an open U so icing fills the top, or an envelope drawn open so a card slides out) when the open shape itself is a recognizable, intentional, friendly choice — not a closed shape with a piece chopped out. If in doubt, draw the clean closed base shape.

If a later stage adds a feature that touches an earlier outline (ears, hair, limbs, tail, mane), the new black feature simply touches that gray outline at its surface. The earlier gray outline stays exactly as it was, and the new black feature is drawn alongside it without crossing it inward. This is the natural way children draw — touching at the edge, not piercing through.

Self-test before finalizing any stage: would a 5-to-8 year old looking only at this stage understand it as a clean recognizable shape? Would they be able to add the next features by simply touching or filling, without erasing and without wondering why a notch is there? If the answer is yes, the stage is well-planned. If the stage looks broken, scooped, slit, or arbitrarily interrupted, redo it as a clean closed shape.
stage_by_stage_script: Stage one (all pure black): draw ONLY the largest one or two base blobs of the character — for example, one oval for the head and one oval for the body, or a single rounded body mass. Plain open outlines in pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}. No face, no eyes, no ears, no limbs, no tail, no mane, no hair, no fur tufts, no wings, no accessories, no decorations, no texture marks. The first-stage shape is drawn as a clean, friendly, closed silhouette with proportions and positioning that already imply where future features will naturally attach.

Stage two: the exact same base blobs from stage one now appear in light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} (unchanged in shape, size, position, orientation). In pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}, add the major structural contours — head contour lines, neck, body contour, limbs, tail, ears, mane outline — whichever large outer contours the character has. Still no face. New external shapes attach naturally along the outside of the previous stage's silhouette by touching it at the surface — the previous outline is never broken, notched, or interrupted to make room for them.

For a four-stage worksheet, stage three (identity stage, around sixty percent through the sequence): all lines from stages one and two now appear in light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} (unchanged in shape and position). In pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}, add the face only — eyes, nose, mouth, simple and minimal, kept child-friendly and easy to reproduce. Facial features sit entirely inside the head shape and the head outline is never modified to accommodate them.

For a four-stage worksheet, stage four (final stage): all lines from stages one, two, and three now appear in light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} (unchanged). In pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}, add only a handful of small finishing details — fur tufts, toes, fingertips, whiskers, tiny spots or stripes in a limited area. The final stage has the LEAST new black content of any stage. All new finishing details sit inside earlier shapes or touch their outlines from outside without requiring any earlier line to be broken, notched, or modified.

For more than four stages, split the middle structural phase and the finishing-details phase across more stages; keep stage one minimal, keep the face-adding identity stage at roughly sixty percent through the sequence, and keep the final stage as small finishing details only.
For three stages, merge the middle two stages: stage one = base blobs, stage two = full body contours plus face, stage three = finishing details.
stage_one_is_critical: Stage one is where most worksheets go wrong. It must be DRASTICALLY simpler than a viewer expects.
Stage one must be so plain that if you hid the other stages, a viewer could not tell what {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} is coming next. It looks like the very first pencil marks on an empty page.
Stage one is plain open outlines only, in pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}. Never a filled shape. Never a solid silhouette. Never a black blob. Only outlines.
Stage one contains no face, no eyes, no ears, no limbs, no tail, no hair, no fur tufts, no mane, no wings, no accessories, no decorations, no texture marks — nothing recognizable.
Stage one is the only stage on the canvas with NO gray lines anywhere. Every other stage must contain at least one gray line.
canvas_and_output: Output resolution: render the image at exactly {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}} — do not upscale, do not super-sample, do not produce any resolution higher than {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}}. The final pixel dimensions of the output image must correspond to {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}}, with crisp sharp linework calibrated for activity-book printing at that resolution.

The canvas is a single open page — no visible panels, no visible frames, no visible boxes, no visible borders, no visible grid lines, no visible dividers of any kind between the stages or around the outer edge.
layout: Place the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} stages in a staggered N-shaped reading flow across the canvas, following the sequence of stages from first to last.

For a four-stage worksheet, use this exact arrangement: the first stage sits in the upper-left area of the canvas; the second stage sits in the lower-left area, below the first stage but shifted slightly to the right so that its center does not sit directly under the first stage; the third stage sits in the upper-right area; the fourth stage sits in the lower-right area, below the third stage but shifted slightly further to the right so that its center does not sit directly under the third stage.
The reading flow goes: first stage → second stage → third stage → fourth stage, tracing a staggered N shape across the canvas.

For a stage count other than four, keep the same staggered N logic — alternating upper and lower positions while progressively drifting from left to right — and distribute the stages evenly across the canvas.

Keep airy, generous spacing between stages with comfortable outer margins around the whole composition. Stages may visually approach each other at their outer edges but the drawn content of one stage must never overlap the drawn content of another stage.

The {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} is anchored at the same relative position and the same scale within every stage area. No shifting, drifting, floating, or recentering of the character between stages — every stage reads as a transparent overlay of the next, same anchor, same scale, only fresh black lines added on top of the gray history.
arrows_critical: Arrows are CRITICAL. Get the count, the color, the style, and the direction exactly right. Do not improvise.

Total arrow count: draw EXACTLY {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} minus 1 arrows on the entire canvas — never more, never fewer. For a four-stage worksheet this means EXACTLY 3 arrows. For a three-stage worksheet, EXACTLY 2 arrows. For a five-stage worksheet, EXACTLY 4 arrows. Count them before finalizing.

Each arrow connects exactly one consecutive pair of stages: arrow 1 goes from stage 1 to stage 2, arrow 2 goes from stage 2 to stage 3, arrow 3 goes from stage 3 to stage 4, and so on. Never draw an arrow between non-consecutive stages. Never draw an arrow from the final stage back to any earlier stage. Never draw a closing or looping arrow that returns to stage 1.

Arrow style: dotted line (a sequence of small round dots evenly spaced), softly curved (a gentle arc, not a sharp angle, not a perfectly straight segment), with a single small simple arrowhead at the destination end only. No double-headed arrows. No solid lines. No dashed lines. No thick painted strokes. No fancy decorative arrows.

Arrow color: every arrow and every arrowhead is exactly {{ARROW_COLOR}} — a soft medium gray. Never pure black. Never the light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} used for previous-stage character lines (arrows must read as a slightly different, slightly darker gray than the gray-history character lines so the eye can tell them apart). Never any other color.

Arrow size: arrows are clearly visible but visually quieter than the character linework. The dot diameter and arrowhead size are noticeably smaller than {{PATH_WIDTH}} so the eye reads the character as the main subject and the arrows as secondary guidance.

Arrow placement: each arrow sits in the empty space between the two stages it connects, following the staggered N reading flow. Arrows never cross any drawn character line, never cross another arrow, and never overlap the silhouette of any stage.

Forbidden arrow mistakes: drawing four or more arrows in a four-stage worksheet; drawing a closing arrow from the final stage; drawing any arrow that loops back; drawing duplicate arrows between the same pair of stages; drawing arrows in pure black; drawing solid or dashed arrows instead of dotted; drawing straight arrows instead of softly curved; drawing arrows with arrowheads at both ends; drawing arrows that cross the character or another arrow.
identity_and_props: The character is the same species, same pose, same expression, same proportions, same silhouette in every stage.

No decorative prop (banana, flower, leaf, heart, star, cloud, food, toy, hat, bow, crown, scarf, glasses) may appear at any stage unless the user explicitly asked for it as part of the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}}. The drawing is the character alone.
Nothing is restyled between stages. No line moves, no proportion changes, no new accessory appears mid-sequence.
progression_balance: The visual change from one stage to the next must be immediately obvious to a child at a glance — never subtle, never minor.
The amount of new black content added at each stage must be roughly equal across the early and middle stages, with the final stage being the smallest addition (small finishing details only).
Do not concentrate the majority of the drawing into one or two stages while leaving other stages nearly unchanged.
Do not apply a large change in one stage followed by only a tiny finishing touch in the next, except for the explicit final-stage finishing details rule.
Every stage transition must feel meaningful and rewarding for the child.
style_and_lines: Drawing style: {{DRAWING_STYLE}}, interpreted in a simplified workbook-friendly way rather than a highly detailed commercial illustration.
Clean two-dimensional cartoon line art, coloring-book-style outlines, smooth, readable, and print-friendly.
Cute, rounded, child-safe shapes appropriate for {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}} unless {{DRAWING_STYLE}} naturally requires a slightly different but still kid-appropriate simplification.
Clear silhouette, simple construction, beginner-friendly, easy to imitate with a pencil or crayon.

No shading, no color fill, no gradients, no gray tones inside shapes, no shadows, no textures, no sketch effect, and no painterly rendering. The only grays on the canvas are the previous-line gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}} on the character and the slightly different arrow gray {{ARROW_COLOR}} on the arrows.
character_design: The {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} must look cute, simple, friendly, and appealing to children in {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}}.
Simplified proportions, open readable shapes, minimal overlaps, and no confusing construction.
Avoid realism, complex anatomy, and excessive detail.
The final character must feel playful, approachable, educational, and confidence-building for kids.
final_checklist: Before finalizing the output, confirm each of the following. If any check fails, redo the worksheet.
Confirm that exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} stages are visible on the canvas.
Confirm that the character in the first stage and the final stage occupy the same silhouette bounding-box area at the same scale.
Confirm that every character line — black or gray — is exactly {{PATH_WIDTH}}, uniform throughout the worksheet, with gray lines NOT thinner or softer than black lines.

Confirm that each stage equals a pixel-identical copy of the previous stage in shape, with the only changes being (a) every previously-black character line is now light gray {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}}, and (b) freshly added character lines of this stage are pure black {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}} — nothing moved, nothing resized, nothing rotated, nothing mirrored, nothing smoothed, nothing simplified, nothing redrawn, nothing retraced, nothing restyled, nothing polished, nothing upgraded, nothing nudged.

Mentally subtract each later stage from its previous stage. Confirm that the only visible differences are the black-to-gray recolor of all previous lines plus the freshly added black lines of that stage. If subtraction reveals any other change to an earlier line beyond the recolor, redo the worksheet.
Confirm that the character's anchor position and overall scale are pixel-identical between every consecutive pair of stages, with no drift in any direction.

Confirm the orientation lock: the character faces the exact same direction in every stage, has not been horizontally mirrored, has not been vertically mirrored, and has not been rotated between any two stages. Every individual line keeps the exact same direction it had when first drawn (curves opening the same way, tail sweeping the same way, face looking the same way). If any stage shows the character or any of its parts mirrored or rotated relative to an earlier stage, redo the worksheet.

Confirm the no-erase rule: every new black line in every later stage either touches an earlier (gray) outline cleanly along its surface from outside, or sits entirely inside an existing closed gray shape — without crossing, breaking, or replacing any earlier line.

Confirm that every base shape in every early stage is a clean, friendly, recognizable closed silhouette — not damaged by awkward notches, slits, scoops, or arbitrary gaps. If a stage looks broken or interrupted in any way, redo it as a clean closed shape.

Confirm the color law: stage one is all pure black with no gray; every stage after stage one contains BOTH gray previous lines AND fresh black lines, with MORE gray than black; the final stage is mostly gray with only a small handful of new black finishing details.
Confirm that no line ever appears in pure black in more than one stage, and no gray line ever turns back to black in a later stage.
Confirm that every individual line within a single stage is entirely black or entirely gray — never partially both, never blended along its length.
Confirm that species, pose, expression, silhouette, and accessories match across every stage with no drift.
Confirm that facial features appear only from the identity stage onward (around sixty percent into the sequence), never in the first or second stage of a four-stage worksheet.

Confirm that the layout follows the staggered N path, with the second stage shifted slightly to the right below the first stage, and the fourth stage shifted slightly to the right below the third stage.
Count the arrows on the canvas. Confirm that the total number of arrows equals exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} minus 1. For a four-stage worksheet this number must be exactly 3.
Confirm that every arrow is dotted (small round dots evenly spaced), softly curved, with a single arrowhead at the destination end only, and is colored exactly {{ARROW_COLOR}}.
Confirm that no arrow connects non-consecutive stages, no arrow loops back from the final stage, and no two arrows connect the same pair of stages.
Confirm that the only ink colors anywhere on the canvas are {{STROKE_COLOR_NEW}}, {{STROKE_COLOR_PREVIOUS}}, and {{ARROW_COLOR}}, with no fills, no other grays, and no other colors.
Confirm that the background is fully {{BACKGROUND}} and that no text, numerals, stage numbers, labels, frames, borders, boxes, grid lines, or dividers appear anywhere on the canvas.
